entries.056b6a35713cbb30756e98043b751df5ed976252: <div sID="gen19008" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="31" osisID="Ezek.31" sID="Ezek.31"/> <div eID="gen19008" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19009" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen19010" type="x-p"/> The prophecy of this chapter, as the two chapters before, is against Egypt, and designed for the humbling and mortifying of Pharaoh. In passing sentence upon great criminals it is usual to consult precedents, and to see what has been done to others in the like case, which serves both to direct and to justify the proceedings. Pharaoh stands indicted at the bar of divine justice for his pride and haughtiness, and the injuries he had done to God's people; but he thinks himself so high, so great, as not to be accountable to any authority, so strong, and so well guarded, as not to be conquerable by any force. The prophet is therefore directed to make a report to him of the case of the king of Assyria, whose head city was Nineveh. I. He must show him how great a monarch the king of Assyria had been, what a vast empire he had, what a mighty sway he bore; the king of Egypt, great as he was could not go beyond him, <reference osisRef="Ezek.31.3-Ezek.31.9">ver. 3-9</reference>. II. He must then show him how like he was to the king of Assyria in pride and carnal security, <reference osisRef="Ezek.31.10">ver. 10</reference>. III. He must next read him the history of the fall and ruin of the king of Assyria, what a noise it made among the nations and what a warning it gave to all potent princes to take heed of pride, <reference osisRef="Ezek.31.11-Ezek.31.17">ver. 11-17</reference>. IV. He must leave the king of Egypt to apply all this to himself, to see his own face in the looking-glass of the king of Assyria's sin, and to foresee his own fall through the perspective glass of his ruin, <reference osisRef="Ezek.31.18">ver. 18</reference>.
entries.bd30603113c3cde39e7b66e781f07f846120ced1: <div eID="gen19010" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen19009" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">The King of Assyria's Greatness. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 588.)</title> <div sID="gen19011" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> And it came to pass in the eleventh year, in the third <hi type="italic">month,</hi> in the first <hi type="italic">day</hi> of the month, <hi type="italic">that</hi> the word of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> came unto me, saying, <hi type="super">2</hi> Son of man, speak unto Pharaoh king of Egypt, and to his multitude; Whom art thou like in thy greatness? <hi type="super">3</hi> Behold, the Assyrian <hi type="italic">was</hi> a cedar in Lebanon with fair branches, and with a shadowing shroud, and of a high stature; and his top was among the thick boughs. <hi type="super">4</hi> The waters made him great, the deep set him up on high with her rivers running round about his plants, and sent out her little rivers unto all the trees of the field. <hi type="super">5</hi> Therefore his height was exalted above all the trees of the field, and his boughs were multiplied, and his branches became long because of the multitude of waters, when he shot forth. <hi type="super">6</hi> All the fowls of heaven made their nests in his boughs, and under his branches did all the beasts of the field bring forth their young, and under his shadow dwelt all great nations. <hi type="super">7</hi> Thus was he fair in his greatness, in the length of his branches: for his root was by great waters. <hi type="super">8</hi> The cedars in the garden of God could not hide him: the fir trees were not like his boughs, and the chestnut-trees were not like his branches; nor any tree in the garden of God was like unto him in his beauty. <hi type="super">9</hi> I have made him fair by the multitude of his branches: so that all the trees of Eden, that <hi type="italic">were</hi> in the garden of God, envied him. <div eID="gen19011" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19012" type="x-p"/> This prophecy bears date the month before Jerusalem was taken, as that in the close of the foregoing chapter about four months before. When God's people were in the depth of their distress, it would be some comfort to them, as it would serve likewise for a check to the pride and malice of their neighbours, that insulted over them, to be told from heaven that the cup was going round, even the cup of trembling, that it would shortly be taken out of the hands of God's people and put into the hands of those that hated them, <reference osisRef="Isa.51.22-Isa.51.23">Isa. li. 22, 23</reference>. In this prophecy, <div eID="gen19012" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19013" type="x-p"/> I. The prophet is directed to put Pharaoh upon searching the records for a case parallel to his own (<reference osisRef="Ezek.31.2">v. 2</reference>): <hi type="italic">Speak to Pharaoh and to his multitude,</hi> to the multitude of his attendants, that contributed so much to his magnificence, and the multitude of his armies, that contributed so much to his strength. These he was proud of, these he put a confidence in; and they were as proud of him and trusted as much in him. Now ask him, <hi type="italic">Whom art thou like in thy greatness?</hi> We are apt to judge of ourselves by comparison. Those that think highly of themselves fancy themselves as great and as good as such and such, that have been mightily celebrated. The flatterers of princes tell them whom they equal in pomp and grandeur. "Well," says God, "let him pitch upon the most famous potentate that ever was, and it shall be allowed that he is <hi type="italic">like him in greatness</hi> and no way inferior to him; but, let him pitch upon whom he will, he will find that <hi type="italic">his day came to fall;</hi> he will see there was <hi type="italic">an end</hi> of all <hi type="italic">his perfection,</hi> and must therefore expect the end of his own in like manner." Note, The falls of others, both into sin and ruin, are intended as admonitions to us not to be secure or <hi type="italic">high-minded,</hi> nor to think we stand out of danger. <div eID="gen19013" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19014" type="x-p"/> II. He is directed to show him an instance of one whom he resembles in greatness, and that was the Assyrian (<reference osisRef="Ezek.31.3">v. 3</reference>), whose monarchy had continued from Nimrod. Sennacherib was one of the mighty princes of that monarchy; but it sunk down soon after him, and the monarchy of Nebuchadnezzar was built upon its ruins, or rather grafted upon its stock. Let us now see what a flourishing prince the king of Assyria was. He is here compared to a stately cedar, <reference osisRef="Ezek.31.3">v. 3</reference>. The glory of the house of David is illustrated by the same similitude, <reference osisRef="Ezek.17.3">ch. xvii. 3</reference>. The olive-tree, the fig-tree, and the vine, which were all fruit-trees, had refused to be <hi type="italic">promoted over the trees</hi> because they would not leave their fruitfulness (<reference osisRef="Judg.9.8">Judg. ix. 8</reference>, &c.), and therefore the choice falls upon the cedar, that is stately and strong, and casts a great shadow, but bears no fruit. 1. The Assyrian monarch was a tall cedar, such as the cedars in Lebanon generally were, of a <hi type="italic">high stature,</hi> and <hi type="italic">his top among the thick boughs;</hi> he was attended by other princes that were tributaries to him, and was surrounded by a life-guard of brave men. He surpassed all the princes in his neighbourhood; they were all shrubs to him (<reference osisRef="Ezek.31.5">v. 5</reference>): <hi type="italic">His height was exalted above all the trees of the field;</hi> they were many of them very high, but he overtopped them all, <reference osisRef="Ezek.31.8">v. 8</reference>. The cedars, even those in the garden of Eden, which we may suppose were the best of the kind, <hi type="italic">would not hide him,</hi> but his top branches outshot theirs. 2. He was a spreading cedar; his branches did not only run up in height, but run out in breadth, denoting that this mighty prince was not only exalted to great dignity and honour, and had a name above the names of the great men of the earth, but that he obtained great dominion and power; his territories were large, and he extended his conquests far and his influences much further. This cedar, like <hi type="italic">a vine,</hi> sent forth <hi type="italic">his branches to the sea, to the river,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.80.11">Ps. lxxx. 11</reference>. <hi type="italic">His boughs were multiplied; his branches became long</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ezek.31.5">v. 5</reference>); so that <hi type="italic">he had a shadowing shroud,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ezek.31.3">v. 3</reference>. This contributed very much to his beauty, that he grew proportionably large as well as high. He was <hi type="italic">fair in his greatness, in the length of his branches</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ezek.31.7">v. 7</reference>), very comely as well as very stately, <hi type="italic">fair by the multitude of his branches,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ezek.31.9">v. 9</reference>. His large dominions were well managed, like a spreading tree that is kept in shape and good order by the skill of the gardener, so as to be very beautiful to the eye. His government was as amiable in the eyes of wise men as it was admirable in the eyes of all men. The <hi type="italic">fir-trees</hi> were not <hi type="italic">like his boughs,</hi> so straight, so green, so regular; nor were the branches of <hi type="italic">the chestnut-trees like his branches,</hi> so thick, so spreading. In short, <hi type="italic">no tree in the garden of God,</hi> in Eden, in Babylon (for that stood where paradise was planted), where there was every tree that was <hi type="italic">pleasant to the sight</hi> (<reference osisRef="Gen.2.9">Gen. ii. 9</reference>), was like <hi type="italic">to this cedar in beauty;</hi> that is, in all the surrounding nations there was no prince so much admired, so much courted, and whom every body was so much in love with, as the king of Assyria. Many of them <hi type="italic">did virtuously,</hi> but he <hi type="italic">excelled them all,</hi> outshone them all. <hi type="italic">All the trees of Eden envied him,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ezek.31.9">v. 9</reference>. When they found they could not compare with him they were angry and grieved that he so far outdid them, and secretly grudged him the praise due to him. Note, It is the unhappiness of those who in any thing excel others that thereby they make themselves the objects of envy; and <hi type="italic">who can stand before envy?</hi> 3. He was serviceable, as far as a standing growing cedar could be, and that was only by his shadow (<reference osisRef="Ezek.31.6">v. 6</reference>): <hi type="italic">All the fowls of heaven,</hi> some of all sorts, <hi type="italic">made their nests in his boughs,</hi> where they were sheltered from the injuries of the weather. The <hi type="italic">beasts of the field</hi> put themselves under the protection of <hi type="italic">his branches.</hi> There they were <hi type="italic">levant—rising up,</hi> and <hi type="italic">couchant—lying down;</hi> there they <hi type="italic">brought forth their young;</hi> for they had there a natural covert from the heat and from the storm. The meaning of all is, <hi type="italic">Under his shadow dwelt all great nations;</hi> they all fled to him for safety, and were willing to swear allegiance to him if he would undertake to protect them, as travellers in a shower come under thick trees for shelter. Note, Those who have power ought to use it for the protection and comfort of those whom they have power over; for to that end they are entrusted with power. Even the bramble, if he be anointed king, invites the trees to come and <hi type="italic">trust in his shadow,</hi> <reference osisRef="Judg.9.15">Judg. ix. 15</reference>. But the utmost security that any creature, even the king of Assyria himself, can give, is but like the shadow of a tree, which is but a scanty and slender protection, and leaves a man many ways exposed. Let us therefore flee to God for protection, and he will take us <hi type="italic">under the shadow of his wings,</hi> where we shall be warmer and safer than under the shadow of the strongest and stateliest cedar, <reference osisRef="Ps.17.8">Ps. xvii. 8</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.91.4">xci. 4</reference>. 4. He seemed to be settled and established in his greatness and power. For, (1.) It was God that <hi type="italic">made him fair,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ezek.31.9">v. 9</reference>. For by him kings reign. He was comely with the comeliness that God put upon him. Note, God's hand must be eyed and owned in the advancement of the great men of the earth, and therefore we must not envy them; yet that will not secure the continuance of their prosperity, for he that gave them their beauty, if they be deprived of it, knows how to turn it into deformity. (2.) He seemed to have a good bottom. This cedar was not like the <hi type="italic">heath in the desert, made to inhabit the parched places</hi> (<reference osisRef="Jer.17.6">Jer. xvii. 6</reference>); it was not a <hi type="italic">root in a dry ground,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.53.2">Isa. liii. 2</reference>. No; he had abundance of wealth to support his power and grandeur (<reference osisRef="Ezek.31.4">v. 4</reference>): <hi type="italic">The waters made him great;</hi> he had vast treasures, large stores and magazines, which were as <hi type="italic">the deep that set him up on high,</hi> constant revenues coming in by taxes, customs, and crown-rents, which were <hi type="italic">as rivers running round about his plants;</hi> these enabled him to strengthen and secure his interests every where, for he <hi type="italic">sent out his little rivers,</hi> or conduits, <hi type="italic">to all the trees of the field,</hi> to water them; and when they had <hi type="italic">maintenance from the king's palace</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ezra.4.14">Ezra iv. 14</reference>), and <hi type="italic">their country was nourished by the king's country</hi> (<reference osisRef="Acts.12.20">Acts xii. 20</reference>), they would be serviceable and faithful to him. Those that have wealth flowing upon them in great rivers find themselves obliged to send it out again in little rivers; for, <hi type="italic">as goods are increased, those are increased that eat them,</hi> and the more men have the more occasion they have for it; yea, and still the more they have occasion for. The <hi type="italic">branches</hi> of this cedar <hi type="italic">became long,</hi> because of <hi type="italic">the multitude of waters</hi> which fed them (<reference osisRef="Ezek.31.5">v. 5</reference> and <reference osisRef="Ezek.31.7">7</reference>); <hi type="italic">his root was by great waters,</hi> which seemed to secure it that <hi type="italic">its leaf should never wither</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.1.3">Ps. i. 3</reference>), that it should not <hi type="italic">see when heat came,</hi> <reference osisRef="Jer.17.8">Jer. xvii. 8</reference>. Note, Worldly people may seem to have an established prosperity, yet it only seems so, <reference osisRef="Job.5.3">Job v. 3</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.37.35">Ps. xxxvii. 35</reference>.
entries.eb79237ac57c32dec82d78d994515874270bb79a: <div eID="gen19014" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">The King of Assyria's Downfall; The Fall of Assyria. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 588.)</title> <div sID="gen19015" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">10</hi> Therefore thus saith the Lord <hi type="small-caps">God</hi> ; Because thou hast lifted up thyself in height, and he hath shot up his top among the thick boughs, and his heart is lifted up in his height; <hi type="super">11</hi> I have therefore delivered him into the hand of the mighty one of the heathen; he shall surely deal with him: I have driven him out for his wickedness. <hi type="super">12</hi> And strangers, the terrible of the nations, have cut him off, and have left him: upon the mountains and in all the valleys his branches are fallen, and his boughs are broken by all the rivers of the land; and all the people of the earth are gone down from his shadow, and have left him. <hi type="super">13</hi> Upon his ruin shall all the fowls of the heaven remain, and all the beasts of the field shall be upon his branches: <hi type="super">14</hi> To the end that none of all the trees by the waters exalt themselves for their height, neither shoot up their top among the thick boughs, neither their trees stand up in their height, all that drink water: for they are all delivered unto death, to the nether parts of the earth, in the midst of the children of men, with them that go down to the pit. <hi type="super">15</hi> Thus saith the Lord <hi type="small-caps">God</hi> ; In the day when he went down to the grave I caused a mourning: I covered the deep for him, and I restrained the floods thereof, and the great waters were stayed: and I caused Lebanon to mourn for him, and all the trees of the field fainted for him. <hi type="super">16</hi> I made the nations to shake at the sound of his fall, when I cast him down to hell with them that descend into the pit: and all the trees of Eden, the choice and best of Lebanon, all that drink water, shall be comforted in the nether parts of the earth. <hi type="super">17</hi> They also went down into hell with him unto <hi type="italic">them that be</hi> slain with the sword; and <hi type="italic">they that were</hi> his arm, <hi type="italic">that</hi> dwelt under his shadow in the midst of the heathen. <hi type="super">18</hi> To whom art thou thus like in glory and in greatness among the trees of Eden? yet shalt thou be brought down with the trees of Eden unto the nether parts of the earth: thou shalt lie in the midst of the uncircumcised with <hi type="italic">them that be</hi> slain by the sword. This <hi type="italic">is</hi> Pharaoh and all his multitude, saith the Lord <hi type="small-caps">God</hi> . <div eID="gen19015" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19016" type="x-p"/> We have seen the king of Egypt resembling the king of Assyria in pomp, and power, and prosperity, how like he was to him in his greatness; now here we see, <div eID="gen19016" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19017" type="x-p"/> I. How he does likewise resemble him in his pride, <reference osisRef="Ezek.31.10">v. 10</reference>. For, as face answers to face in a glass, so does one corrupt carnal heart to another; and the same temptations of a prosperous state by which some are overcome are fatal to many others too. "<hi type="italic">Thou,</hi> O king of Egypt! <hi type="italic">hast lifted up thyself in height,</hi> hast been proud of thy wealth and power, <reference osisRef="Ezek.29.3">ch. xxix. 3</reference>. And just so <hi type="italic">he</hi> (that is, the king of Assyria); when he had <hi type="italic">shot up his top among the thick boughs his heart</hi> was immediately <hi type="italic">lifted up in his height,</hi> and he grew insolent and imperious, set God himself at defiance, and trampled upon his people;" witness the messages and letter which <hi type="italic">the great king, the king of Assyria,</hi> sent to Hezekiah, <reference osisRef="Isa.36.4">Isa. xxxvi. 4</reference>. How haughtily does he speak of himself and his own achievements! how scornfully of that great and good man! There were other sins in which the Egyptians and the Assyrians did concur, particularly that of oppressing God's people, which is charged upon them both together (<reference osisRef="Isa.52.4">Isa. lii. 4</reference>); but here that sin is traced up to its cause, and that was pride; for it is the <hi type="italic">contempt of the proud</hi> that they are <hi type="italic">filled with.</hi> Note, When men's outward condition rises their minds commonly rise with it; and it is very rare to find a humble spirit in the midst of great advancements. <div eID="gen19017" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19018" type="x-p"/> II. How he shall therefore resemble him in his fall; and for the opening of this part of the comparison, <div eID="gen19018" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19019" type="x-p"/> 1. Here is a history of the fall of the king of Assyria. For his part, says God (<reference osisRef="Ezek.31.11">v. 11</reference>), <hi type="italic">I have therefore,</hi> because he was thus lifted up, <hi type="italic">delivered him into the hand of the mighty one of the heathen.</hi> Cyaxares, king of the Medes, in the twenty-sixth year of his reign, in conjunction with Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon in the first year of his reign, destroyed Nineveh, and with it the Assyrian empire. Nebuchadnezzar, though he was not then, yet afterwards became, very emphatically, the <hi type="italic">mighty one of the heathen,</hi> most mighty among them and most mighty over them, to prevail against them. <div eID="gen19019" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19020" type="x-p"/> (1.) Respecting the fall of the Assyrian three things are affirmed:—[1.] It is God himself that orders his ruin: <hi type="italic">I have delivered him into the hand</hi> of the executioner; <hi type="italic">I have driven him out.</hi> Note, God is the Judge, who puts down one and sets up another (<reference osisRef="Ps.75.7">Ps. lxxv. 7</reference>); and when he pleases he can extirpate and expel those who think themselves, and seem to others, to have taken deepest root. And the mightiest ones of the heathens could not gain their point against those they contended with if the Almighty did not himself deliver them into their hands. [2.] It is his own sin that procures his ruin: <hi type="italic">I have driven him out for his wickedness.</hi> None are driven out from their honour, power, and possessions, but it is <hi type="italic">for their wickedness.</hi> None of our comforts are ever lost but what have been a thousand times forfeited. If the wicked are <hi type="italic">driven away,</hi> it is <hi type="italic">in their wickedness.</hi> [3.] It is a <hi type="italic">mighty one of the heathen</hi> that shall be the instrument of his ruin; for God often employs one wicked man in punishing another. <hi type="italic">He shall surely deal with him,</hi> shall know how to manage him, great as he is. Note, Proud imperious men will, sooner or later, meet with their match. <div eID="gen19020" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19021" type="x-p"/> (2.) In this history of the fall of the Assyrian observe, [1.] A continuation of the similitude of the cedar. He grew very high, and extended his boughs very far; but his day comes to fall. <hi type="italic">First,</hi> This stately cedar was cropped: <hi type="italic">The terrible of the nations cut him off.</hi> Soldiers, who being both armed and commissioned to kill, and slay, and destroy, may well be reckoned among <hi type="italic">the terrible of the nations.</hi> They have lopped off his branches first, have seized upon some parts of his dominion and forced them out of his hands; so that in all <hi type="italic">mountains</hi> and <hi type="italic">valleys</hi> of the nations about, in the high-lands and low-lands, and <hi type="italic">by all the rivers,</hi> there were cities or countries that were broken off from the Assyrian monarchy, that had been subject to it, but had either revolted or were recovered from it. Its feathers were borrowed; and, when every bird had fetched back its own, it was naked like the stump of a tree. <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> It was deserted: <hi type="italic">All the people of the earth,</hi> that had fled to him for shelter, have <hi type="italic">gone down from his shadow and have left him.</hi> When he was disabled to give them protection they thought they no longer owed him allegiance. Let not great men be proud of the number of those that attend them and have a dependence upon them; it is only for what they can get. When Providence frowns upon them their retinue is soon dispersed and scattered from them. <hi type="italic">Thirdly,</hi> It was insulted over, and its fall triumphed in (<reference osisRef="Ezek.31.13">v. 13</reference>): <hi type="italic">Upon his ruin shall all the fowls of the heaven remain,</hi> to tread upon the broken branches of this cedar. Its fall is triumphed in by the other trees, who were angry to see themselves overtopped so much: <hi type="italic">All the trees of Eden,</hi> that were cut down and had fallen before him, <hi type="italic">all that drank water</hi> of the rain of heaven, as the stump of the tree that is left in the <hi type="italic">south</hi> is said to be <hi type="italic">wet with the dew of heaven</hi> (<reference osisRef="Dan.4.23">Dan. iv. 23</reference>) and to bud <hi type="italic">through the scent of water</hi> (<reference osisRef="Job.14.9">Job xiv. 9</reference>), <hi type="italic">shall be comforted in the nether parts of the earth</hi> when they see this proud cedar brought as low as themselves. <hi type="italic">Solamen miseris socios habuisse doloris</hi>—<hi type="italic">To have companions in woe is a solace to those who suffer.</hi> But, on the contrary, the trees of Lebanon, that are yet standing in their height and strength, <hi type="italic">mourned for him,</hi> and <hi type="italic">the trees of the field fainted for him,</hi> because they could not but read their own destiny in his fall. <hi type="italic">Howl, fir-trees, if the cedar be shaken,</hi> for they cannot expect to stand long, <reference osisRef="Zech.11.2">Zech. xi. 2</reference>. [2.] An explanation of the similitude of the cedar. By the cutting down of this cedar is signified the slaughter of this mighty monarch and all his adherents and supporters; they are all <hi type="italic">delivered to death,</hi> to fall by the sword, as the cedar by the axe. He and his princes, who, he said, were <hi type="italic">altogether kings,</hi> go down to the grave, <hi type="italic">to the nether parts of the earth, in the midst of the children of men,</hi> as common persons of no quality or distinction. <hi type="italic">They died like men</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.82.7">Ps. lxxxii. 7</reference>); they were carried away with <hi type="italic">those that go down to the pit,</hi> and their pomp did neither protect them nor <hi type="italic">descend after them.</hi> Again (<reference osisRef="Ezek.31.16">v. 16</reference>), He was <hi type="italic">cast down to hell with those that descend into the pit;</hi> he went into the state of the dead, and was buried as others are, in obscurity and oblivion. Again (<reference osisRef="Ezek.31.17">v. 17</reference>), <hi type="italic">They all that were his arm,</hi> on whom he stayed, by whom he acted and exerted his power, all <hi type="italic">that dwelt under his shadow,</hi> his subjects and allies, and all that had any dependence on him, they all <hi type="italic">went down</hi> into ruin, down into the grace <hi type="italic">with him, unto those that were slain with the sword,</hi> to those that were cut off by untimely deaths before them, under the load of guilt and shame. When great men fall a great many fall with them, as a great many in like manner have fallen before them. [3.] What God designed, and aimed at, in bringing down this mighty monarch and his monarchy. He designed thereby, <hi type="italic">First, To give an alarm</hi> to the nations about, to put them all to a stand, to put them all to a gaze (<reference osisRef="Ezek.31.16">v. 16</reference>): <hi type="italic">I made the nations to shake at the sound of his fall.</hi> They were all struck with astonishment to see so mighty a prince brought down thus. It give a shock to all their confidences, every one thinking his turn would be next. <hi type="italic">When he went down to the grave</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ezek.31.15">v. 15</reference>) <hi type="italic">I caused a mourning,</hi> a general lamentation, as the whole kingdom goes into mourning at the death of the king. In token of this general grief, <hi type="italic">I covered the deep for him,</hi> put that into black, gave a stop to business, in complaisance to this universal mourning. <hi type="italic">I restrained the floods, and the great waters were stayed,</hi> that they might run into another channel, that of lamentation. Lebanon particularly, the kingdom of Syria, that was sometimes in confederacy with the Assyrian, mourned for him; as the allies of Babylon, <reference osisRef="Rev.18.9">Rev. xviii. 9</reference>. <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> To give an admonition to the nations about, and to their kings (<reference osisRef="Ezek.31.14">v. 14</reference>): <hi type="italic">To the end that none of all the trees by the waters,</hi> though ever so advantageously situated, <hi type="italic">may exalt themselves for their height,</hi> may be proud and conceited of themselves and <hi type="italic">shoot up their top among the thick boughs,</hi> looking disdainfully upon others, nor <hi type="italic">stand upon themselves for their height,</hi> confiding in their own politics and powers, as if they could never be brought down. Let them all take warning by the Assyrian, for he once held up his head as high, and thought he kept his footing as firm, as any of them; but his pride went before his destruction, and his confidence failed him. Note, The fall of proud presumptuous men is intended for warning to others to keep humble. It would have been well for Nebuchadnezzar, who was himself active in bringing down the Assyrian, if he had taken the admonition. <div eID="gen19021" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19022" type="x-p"/> 2. Here is a prophecy of the fall of the king of Egypt in like manner, <reference osisRef="Ezek.31.18">v. 18</reference>. He thought himself like the Assyrian <hi type="italic">in glory and greatness,</hi> over-topping <hi type="italic">all the trees of Eden,</hi> as the cypress does the shrubs. "But <hi type="italic">thou</hi> also <hi type="italic">shalt be brought down,</hi> with the other trees that are pleasant to the sight, as those in Eden. Thou shalt be <hi type="italic">brought to the grave,</hi> to the nether or lower <hi type="italic">parts of the earth;</hi> thou shalt <hi type="italic">lie in the midst of the uncircumcised,</hi> that die in their uncleanness, die ingloriously, die under a curse and at a distance from God; then shall those whom thou hast trampled upon triumph over thee, saying, <hi type="italic">This is Pharaoh and all his multitude.</hi> See how mean he looks, how low he lies; see what all his pomp and pride have come to; here is all that is left of him." Note, Great men and great multitudes, with the great figure and great noise they make in the world, when God comes to contend with them, will soon become little, less than nothing, such as Pharaoh and all his multitude.  <chapter eID="Ezek.31"/> <div eID="gen19022" type="x-p"/>

entries.90a593237853f6b40194b32beaa9e01c3bd84c64: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11609"/><title type="x-s2">CHAPTER 31</title> <title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Ezek.31.1-Ezek.31.18">Eze 31:1-18</reference>. The Overthrow of Egypt Illustrated by That of Assyria.</title> <div sID="gen21032" type="x-p"/> Not that Egypt was, like Assyria, utterly to cease to be, but it was, like Assyria, to lose its prominence in the empire of the world.<div eID="gen21032" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21033" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11609"/><hi type="bold">1. third month--</hi>two months later than the prophecy delivered in <reference osisRef="Ezek.30.20">Eze 30:20</reference>. <div eID="gen21033" type="x-p"/>
entries.0b38d4c374e1b46c975a4c73689f74aa3dfdea3e: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11610"/><div sID="gen21034" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11610"/><hi type="bold">2. Whom art thou like--</hi>The answer is, Thou art like the haughty king of Assyria; as he was overthrown by the Chaldeans, so shalt thou be by the same. <div eID="gen21034" type="x-p"/>
entries.a33b30c044c0e4688fdf47499d7261262ac3596d: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11611"/><div sID="gen21035" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11611"/>3. He illustrates the pride and the consequent overthrow of the Assyrian, that Egypt may the better know what she must expect.<div eID="gen21035" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21036" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">cedar in Lebanon--</hi>often eighty feet high, and the diameter of the space covered by its boughs still greater: the symmetry perfect. Compare the similar image (<reference osisRef="Ezek.17.3">Eze 17:3</reference>; <reference osisRef="Dan.4.20-Dan.4.22">Da 4:20-22</reference>).<div eID="gen21036" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21037" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">with a shadowing shroud--</hi>with an overshadowing thicket.<div eID="gen21037" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21038" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">top ... among ... thick boughs--</hi>rather [Hengstenberg], "among the clouds." But English Version agrees better with the Hebrew. The top, or topmost shoot, represents the king; the thick boughs, the large resources of the empire. <div eID="gen21038" type="x-p"/>
entries.adaa3ca5c1e1fb6e3c781ba95a703eba5beeb084: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11612"/><div sID="gen21039" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11612"/><hi type="bold">4. waters ... little rivers--</hi>the Tigris with its branches and "rivulets," or "conduits" for irrigation, the source of Assyria's fertility. "The deep" is the ever flowing water, never dry. Metaphorically, for Assyria's resources, as the "conduits" are her colonies. <div eID="gen21039" type="x-p"/>
entries.cf72442ad648cb8618eeafca5e37baebe5e8d76c: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11613"/><div sID="gen21040" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11613"/><hi type="bold">5. when he shot forth--</hi>because of the abundant moisture which nourished him in shooting forth. But see Margin. <div eID="gen21040" type="x-p"/>
entries.c4cca1c883f204b356a1366d4b3ed4a87a125a9a: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11614"/><div sID="gen21041" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11614"/><hi type="bold">6. fowls ... made ... nests in ... boughs--</hi>so <reference osisRef="Ezek.17.23">Eze 17:23</reference>; <reference osisRef="Dan.4.12">Da 4:12</reference>. The gospel kingdom shall gather all under its covert, for their good and for the glory of God, which the world kingdoms did for evil and for self-aggrandizement (<reference osisRef="Matt.13.32">Mt 13:32</reference>). <div eID="gen21041" type="x-p"/>
entries.18f847286850cf081407109bab5ce08b39c2470f: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11615"/><div sID="gen21042" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11615"/><hi type="bold">8. cedars ... could not hide him--</hi>could not outtop him. No other king eclipsed him.<div eID="gen21042" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21043" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">were not like--</hi>were not comparable to.<div eID="gen21043" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21044" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">garden of God--</hi>As in the case of Tyre (<reference osisRef="Ezek.28.13">Eze 28:13</reference>), the imagery, that is applied to the Assyrian king, is taken from Eden; peculiarly appropriate, as Eden was watered by rivers that afterwards watered Assyria (<reference osisRef="Gen.2.10-Gen.2.14">Ge 2:10-14</reference>). This cedar seemed to revive in itself all the glories of paradise, so that no tree there outtopped it. <div eID="gen21044" type="x-p"/>
entries.6125c9dc6280eee93977787d479d9161624e2692: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11616"/><div sID="gen21045" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11616"/><hi type="bold">9. I ... made him--</hi>It was all due to My free grace. <div eID="gen21045" type="x-p"/>
entries.802f15d8f7f257fe2e73020d3253c7efc620bcaf: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11617"/><div sID="gen21046" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11617"/><hi type="bold">10. thou ... he--</hi>The change of persons is because the language refers partly to the cedar, partly to the person signified by the cedar. <div eID="gen21046" type="x-p"/>
entries.842f7a99f8fe74c14249ff545b6b7ba0326a1a02: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11618"/><div sID="gen21047" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11618"/>11. Here the literal supersedes the figurative.<div eID="gen21047" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21048" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">shall surely deal with him--</hi>according to his own pleasure, and according to the Assyrian's (Sardanapalus) desert. Nebuchadnezzar is called "the mighty one" (El, a name of God), because he was God's representative and instrument of judgment (<reference osisRef="Dan.2.37">Da 2:37</reference>, 38). <div eID="gen21048" type="x-p"/>
entries.da86ef3a219428e4191ac84cf020d541117390ab: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11619"/><div sID="gen21049" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11619"/><hi type="bold">12. from his shadow--</hi>under which they had formerly dwelt as their covert (<reference osisRef="Ezek.31.6">Eze 31:6</reference>). <div eID="gen21049" type="x-p"/>
entries.7acf0da809f0b58b703a2f32be42da2b4ae85f93: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11620"/><div sID="gen21050" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11620"/>13. Birds and beasts shall insult over his fallen trunk. <div eID="gen21050" type="x-p"/>
entries.41475898d41362de6ce1ac51bad9bfbe3860ed93: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11621"/><div sID="gen21051" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11621"/><hi type="bold">14. trees by the waters--</hi>that is, that are plentifully supplied by the waters: nations abounding in resources.<div eID="gen21051" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21052" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">stand up in their height--</hi>that is, trust in their height: stand upon it as their ground of confidence. Fairbairn points the Hebrew differently, so as for "their trees," to translate, "(And that none that drink water may stand) on themselves, (because of their greatness)." But the usual reading is better, as Assyria and the confederate states throughout are compared to strong trees. The clause, "All that drink water," marks the ground of the trees' confidence "in their height," namely, that they have ample sources of supply. Maurer, retaining the same Hebrew, translates, "that neither their terebinth trees may stand up in their height, nor all (the other trees) that drink water."<div eID="gen21052" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21053" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">to ... nether ... earth ... pit--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Ezek.32.18">Eze 32:18</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.82.7">Psa 82:7</reference>). <div eID="gen21053" type="x-p"/>
entries.1107def596f4012303abcd6eea456c82637d5a34: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11622"/><div sID="gen21054" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11622"/><hi type="bold">15. covered the deep--</hi>as mourners cover their heads in token of mourning, "I made the deep that watered the cedar" to wrap itself in mourning for him. The waters of the deep are the tributary peoples of Assyria (<reference osisRef="Rev.17.15">Re 17:15</reference>).<div eID="gen21054" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21055" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">fainted--</hi>literally, were "faintness" (itself); more forcible than the verb. <div eID="gen21055" type="x-p"/>
entries.8bf98e433633a0b0507275418b654b6366edb358: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11623"/><div sID="gen21056" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11623"/><hi type="bold">16. hell--</hi>Sheol or Hades, the unseen world: equivalent to, "I cast him into oblivion" (compare <reference osisRef="Isa.14.9-Isa.14.11">Is 14:9-11</reference>).<div eID="gen21056" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21057" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">shall be comforted--</hi>because so great a king as the Assyrian is brought down to a level with them. It is a kind of consolation to the wretched to have companions in misery. <div eID="gen21057" type="x-p"/>
entries.ce3aa7f5c6e8b400875a5243ce9233c0fc777715: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11624"/><div sID="gen21058" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11624"/><hi type="bold">17. his arm, that dwelt under his shadow--</hi>those who were the helpers or tool of his tyranny, and therefore enjoyed his protection (for example, Syria and her neighbors). These were sure to share her fate. Compare the same phrase as to the Jews living under the protection of their king (<reference osisRef="Lam.4.20">La 4:20</reference>); both alike "making flesh their arm, and in heart departing from the Lord" (<reference osisRef="Jer.17.5">Jr 17:5</reference>). <div eID="gen21058" type="x-p"/>
entries.a1e9cbff11258a72a1e6cd9ec093e18467feb34e: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11625"/><div sID="gen21059" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11625"/>18. Application of the parabolic description of Assyria to the parallel case of Egypt. "All that has been said of the Assyrian consider as said to thyself. To whom art thou so like, as thou art to the Assyrian? To none." The lesson on a gigantic scale of Eden-like privileges abused to pride and sin by the Assyrian, as in the case of the first man in Eden, ending in ruin, was to be repeated in Egypt's case. For the unchangeable God governs the world on the same unchangeable principles.<div eID="gen21059" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21060" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">thou shall lie in ... uncircumcised--</hi>As circumcision was an object of mocking to thee, thou shall lie in the midst of the uncircumcised, slain by their sword [Grotius]. Retribution in kind (<reference osisRef="Ezek.28.10">Eze 28:10</reference>).<div eID="gen21060" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21061" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">This is Pharaoh--</hi>Pharaoh's end shall be the same humiliating one as I have depicted the Assyrian's to have been. "This" is demonstrative, as if he were pointing with the finger to Pharaoh lying prostrate, a spectacle to all, as on the shore of the Red Sea (<reference osisRef="Exod.14.30">Ex 14:30</reference>, <reference osisRef="Exod.14.31">31</reference>). <chapter eID="Ezek.31"/>

entries.7fe8ec7d387db9bebea7936af8da5431285d1ed1: <div eID="gen32179" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen32180" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen32181" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen32181" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen32180" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen32182" type="x-p"/> This very beautiful chapter relates also to Egypt. The prophet describes to Pharaoh the fall of the king of Nineveh, (see the books of Nahum, Jonah, and Zephaniah), under the image of a fair cedar of Lebanon, once exceedingly tall, flourishing, and majestic, but now cut down and withered, with its broken branches strewed around, vv. 1-17. He then concludes with bringing the matter home to the king of Egypt, by telling him that this was a picture of his approaching fate, <reference osisRef="Eze.31.18">Eze 31:18</reference>. The beautiful cedar of Lebanon, remarkable for its loftiness, and in the most flourishing condition, but afterwards cut down and deserted, gives a very lately painting of the great glory and dreadful catastrophe of both the Assyrian and Egyptian monarchies. The manner in which the prophet has embellished his subject is deeply interesting; the colouring is of that kind which the mind will always contemplate with pleasure. <div eID="gen32182" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32183" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">Verse 1</hi> <div eID="gen32183" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32184" type="x-p"/> In the eleventh year - On Sunday, June 19, A.M. 3416, according to Abp. Usher; a month before Jerusalem was taken by the Chaldeans.
entries.2a4820de92b355f7fda5fb88c370d30b0bf6738c: <hi type="bold">Verse 3</hi> <div eID="gen32184" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32185" type="x-p"/> Behold, the Assyrian was a cedar - Why is the Assyrian introduced here, when the whole chapter concerns Egypt? Bp. Lowth has shown that אשור ארז ashshur erez should be translated the tall cedar, the very stately cedar; hence there is reference to his lofty top; and all the following description belongs to Egypt, not to Assyria. But see on <reference osisRef="Eze.31.11">Eze 31:11</reference> (note).
entries.0576a8ece37cca1e9bbacf2b0496aa1c366fa506: <hi type="bold">Verse 4</hi> <div eID="gen32185" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32186" type="x-p"/> The waters made him great - Alluding to the fertility of Egypt by the overflowing of the Nile. But waters often mean peoples. By means of the different nations under the Egyptians, that government became very opulent. These nations are represented as fowls and beasts, taking shelter under the protection of this great political Egyptian tree, <reference osisRef="Eze.31.6">Eze 31:6</reference>.
entries.4d82a360e1cd91caa046cc30628cca4284d05982: <hi type="bold">Verse 8</hi> <div eID="gen32186" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32187" type="x-p"/> The cedars in the garden of God - Egypt was one of the most eminent and affluent of all the neighboring nations.
entries.b1c7f9fcf9f2838febbdb0d0648e43233ac6bee5: <hi type="bold">Verse 11</hi> <div eID="gen32187" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32188" type="x-p"/> The mighty one of the heathen - Nebuchadnezzar. It is worthy of notice, that Nebuchadnezzar, in the first year of his reign, rendered himself master of Nineveh, the capital of the Assyrian empire. See Sedar Olam. This happened about twenty years before Ezekiel delivered this prophecy; on this account, Ashshur, <reference osisRef="Eze.31.3">Eze 31:3</reference>, may relate to the Assyrians, to whom it is possible the prophet here compares the Egyptians. But see the note on <reference osisRef="Eze.31.3">Eze 31:3</reference>.
entries.2dbcde21efde77de773803f5dab4415aa53d0064: <hi type="bold">Verse 13</hi> <div eID="gen32188" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32189" type="x-p"/> Upon his ruin shall all the fowls - The fall of Egypt is likened to the fall of a great tree; and as the fowls and beasts sheltered under its branches before, <reference osisRef="Eze.31.6">Eze 31:6</reference>, so they now feed upon its ruins.
entries.baff8d4ee8380bd9a9b85a240a2448e6b4d560d1: <hi type="bold">Verse 14</hi> <div eID="gen32189" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32190" type="x-p"/> To the end that none of all the trees - Let this ruin, fallen upon Egypt, teach all the nations that shall hear of it to be humble, because, however elevated, God can soon bring them down; and pride and arrogance, either in states or individuals, have the peculiar abhorrence of God. Pride does not suit the sons of men; it made devils of angels, and makes fiends of men.
entries.ef8d21d87f5f6000e09931350a91af2d8e46a590: <hi type="bold">Verse 15</hi> <div eID="gen32190" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32191" type="x-p"/> I caused Lebanon to mourn for him - All the confederates of Pharaoh are represented as deploring his fall, <reference osisRef="Eze.31.16">Eze 31:16</reference>, <reference osisRef="Eze.31.17">Eze 31:17</reference>.
entries.c3bdd50713451cef2ca4687823f0c9e70e174053: <hi type="bold">Verse 17</hi> <div eID="gen32191" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32192" type="x-p"/> They also went down into hell with him - Into remediless destruction.
entries.7c5057652aa9c9e428cad1b76e35b708327ca3af: <hi type="bold">Verse 18</hi> <div eID="gen32192" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32193" type="x-p"/> This is Pharaoh - All that I have spoken in this allegory of the lofty cedar refers to Pharaoh, king of Egypt, his princes, confederates, and people. Calmet understands the whole chapter of the king of Assyria, under which he allows that Egypt is adumbrated; and hence on this verse he quotes: - <div eID="gen32193" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32194" type="x-p"/> Mutato nomine, de te fabula narratur. <div eID="gen32194" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32195" type="x-p"/> What is said of Assyria belongs to thee, O Egypt.  <chapter eID="Ezek.31"/> <div eID="gen32195" type="x-p"/>

entries.17230f6ce227474f2c7e05599efb98b862e6f398: <div eID="gen15097" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s2">The Glory and Fall of Asshur a Type of Egypt</title> <div sID="gen15098" type="x-p"/> In two months <hi type="italic">minus</hi> six days from the time when the preceding word of God was uttered, Ezekiel received another threatening word against the king and the people of Egypt, in which the former announcement of the destruction of the might of Egypt was confirmed by a comparison drawn between the power of Egypt and that of Asshur. Ezekiel having opened his prophecy with the question, whom does Pharaoh with his might resemble (<reference osisRef="Ezek.31.2">Eze 31:2</reference>), proceeds to depict Asshur as a mighty towering cedar (<reference osisRef="Ezek.31.3-Ezek.31.9">Eze 31:3-9</reference>) which has been felled and cast down by the prince of the nations on account of its height and pride (<reference osisRef="Ezek.31.10-Ezek.31.14">Eze 31:10-14</reference>), so that everything mourned over its fall, because many nations went down with it to hell (<reference osisRef="Ezek.31.15-Ezek.31.17">Eze 31:15-17</reference>). The question, whom Pharaoh resembles, is then repeated in <reference osisRef="Ezek.31.18">Eze 31:18</reference>; and from the preceding comparison the conclusion is drawn, that he will perish like that lofty cedar. - The reminiscence of the greatness of the Assyrian empire and of its destruction was well adapted to overthrow all reliance upon the might and greatness of Egypt. The fall of that great empire was still so fresh in the mind at the time, that the reminiscence could not fail to make a deep impression upon the prophet’s hearers. <div eID="gen15098" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15099" type="x-p"/> <reference osisRef="Ezek.31.1-Ezek.31.9">Eze 31:1-9</reference> <div eID="gen15099" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15100" type="x-p"/> The might of Pharaoh resembles the greatness and glory of Asshur. - Eze 31:1. <hi type="italic">In the eleventh year, in the third (month), on the first of the month, the word of Jehovah came to me, saying,</hi> Eze 31:2. <hi type="italic">Son of man, say to Pharaoh the king of Egypt, and to his tumult, Whom art thou like in thy greatness?</hi> Eze 31:3. <hi type="italic">Behold, Asshur was a cedar-tree upon Lebanon, beautiful in branches, a shadowing thicket, and its top was high in growth, and among the clouds.</hi> Eze 31:4. <hi type="italic">Water brought him up, the flood made him high, its streams went round about its plantation, and it sent its channels to all the trees of the field.</hi> Eze 31:5. <hi type="italic">Therefore its growth became higher than all the trees of the field, and its branches became great, and its boughs long from many waters in its shooting out.</hi> Eze 31:6. <hi type="italic">In its branches all the birds of the heaven made their nests, and under its boughs all the beasts of the field brought forth, and in its shadow sat great nations of all kinds.</hi> Eze 31:7. <hi type="italic">And he was beautiful in his greatness, in the length of his shoots; for his root was by many waters.</hi> Eze 31:8. <hi type="italic">Cedars did not obscure him in the garden of God, cypresses did not resemble his branches, and plane-trees were not like his boughs; no tree in the garden of God resembled him in his beauty.</hi> Eze 31:9. <hi type="italic">I had made him beautiful in the multitude of his shoots, and all the trees of Eden which were in the garden of God envied him.</hi> - The word of God is addressed to King Pharaoh and to המונו, his tumult, i.e., whoever and whatever occasions noise and tumult in the land. We must not interpret this, however, as Hitzig has done, as signifying the ruling classes and estates in contrast with the quiet in the land, for no such use of המון is anywhere to be found. Nor must we regard the word as applying to the multitude of people only, but to the people with their possessions, their riches, which gave rise to luxury and tumult, as in Eze 30:10. The inquiry, whom does Pharaoh with his tumult resemble in his greatness, is followed in the place of a reply by a description of Asshur as a glorious cedar (<reference osisRef="Ezek.31.3-Ezek.31.9">Eze 31:3-9</reference>). It is true that Ewald has followed the example of Meibom (<hi type="italic">vanarum in Cod. Hebr. interprett. spec.</hi> III p. 70) and J. D. Michaelis, and endeavours to set aside the allusion to Asshur, by taking the word אשּׁוּר in an appellative sense, and understanding אשּׁוּר ארז as signifying a particular kind of cedar, namely, the tallest species of all. But apart altogether from there being no foundation whatever for such an explanation in the usage of the language, there is nothing in the fact to justify it. For it is not anywhere affirmed that Pharaoh resembled this cedar; on the contrary, the question, whom does he resemble? is asked again in <reference osisRef="Ezek.31.18">Eze 31:18</reference> (Hitzig). Moreover, Michaelis is wrong in the supposition that “from <reference osisRef="Ezek.31.10">Eze 31:10</reference> onwards it becomes perfectly obvious that it is not Assyria but Egypt itself which is meant by the cedar-tree previously described.” Under the figure of the felling of a cedar there is depicted the overthrow of a king or monarchy, which has already taken place. Compare <reference osisRef="Ezek.31.12">Eze 31:12</reference> and <reference osisRef="Ezek.31.16">Eze 31:16</reference>, where the past is indicated quite as certainly as the future in Eze 31:18. And as <reference osisRef="Ezek.31.18">Eze 31:18</reference> plainly designates the overthrow of Pharaoh and his power as still in the future, the cedar, whose destruction is not only threatened in <reference osisRef="Ezek.31.10-Ezek.31.17">Eze 31:10-17</reference>, but declared to have already taken place, can only be Asshur, and not Egypt at all. <div eID="gen15100" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15101" type="x-p"/> The picture of the glory of this cedar recalls in several respects the similar figurative description in Ezekiel 17. Asshur is called a cedar upon Lebanon, because it was there that the most stately cedars grew. חרשׁ מצל, a shade-giving thicket (מצל is a <hi type="italic">Hiphil</hi> participle of צלל), belongs to יפה ענף as a further expansion of ענף, corresponding to the further expansion of גּבהּ קמה by “its top was among the clouds.” If we bear this in mind, the reasons assigned by Hitzig for altering חרשׁ into an adjective הרשׁ, and taking מצל as a substantive formation after the analogy of מסב, lose all their force. Analogy would only require an adjective in the construct state in the event of the three statements 'יפה ע, 'הרשׁ מ, and 'גּבהּ גּבהּ ק being co-ordinate with one another. But what is decisive against the proposed conjecture is the fact that neither the noun מצל nor the adjective הרשׁ is ever met with, and that, in any case, מצל cannot signify foliage. The rendering of the Vulgate, “<hi type="italic">frondibus nemorosus</hi>,” is merely guessed at, whilst the Seventy have omitted the word as unintelligible to them. For עבתים, thicket of clouds, see the comm. on <reference osisRef="Ezek.19.11">Eze 19:11</reference>; and for צמּרת, that on Eze 17:3. The cedar grew to so large a size because it was richly watered (<reference osisRef="Ezek.31.4">Eze 31:4</reference>). A flood poured its streams round about the place where the cedar was planted, and sent out brooks to all the trees of the field. The difficult words את־נהרתיה וגו' are to be taken literally thus: as for its (the flood’s) streams, it (the flood) was going round about its plantation, i.e., round about the plantation belonging to the flood or the place situated near it, where the cedar was planted. את is not to be taken as a preposition, but as a sign of the accusative, and את־נהרתיה dna , as an accusative used for the more precise definition of the manner in which the flood surrounded the plantation. It is true that there still remains something striking in the masculine הלך, since תּהום, although of common gender, is construed throughout as a feminine, even in this very verse. But the difficulty remains even if we follow Ewald, and take הלך to be a defectively written or irregular form of the <hi type="italic">Hiphil</hi> הוליך; a conjecture which is precluded by the use of הוליך, to cause to run = to cause to flow away, in Eze 32:14. מטּעהּ, its (the flood’s) plantation, i.e., the plantation for which the flood existed. תּהום is used here to signify the source of starting-point of a flood, as in <reference osisRef="Deut.8.7">Deu 8:7</reference>, where תּהמות are co-ordinate with עינות. - While the place where the cedar was planted was surrounded by the streams of the flood, only the brooks and channels of this flood reached to the trees of the field. The cedar therefore surpassed all the trees of the field in height and luxuriance of growth (<reference osisRef="Ezek.31.5">Eze 31:5</reference>). fגּבהאheb>, an Aramean mode of spelling for גּבהה heb>; and asרעפּתheb>, ἁπ. λεγ.., an Aramean formation with ר inserted, for סעפת, branches. For פּארת, see the comm. on Eze 17:6. בּשׁלּחו cannot mean “since it (the stream) sent out the water” (Ewald); for although תּהום in <reference osisRef="Ezek.31.4">Eze 31:4</reference> is also construed as a masculine, the suffix cannot be taken as referring to תּהום, for this is much too far off. And the explanation proposed by Rosenmüller, Hävernick, Kliefoth, and others, “as it (the tree) sent them (the branches) out,” is open to this objection, that בּשׁלּחו would then contain a spiritless tautology; since the stretching out of the branches is already contained in the fact of their becoming numerous and long. the tautology has no existence if the object is left indefinite, “in its spreading out,” i.e., the spreading not only of the branches, but also of the roots, to which שׁלּח is sometimes applied (cf. <reference osisRef="Jer.17.8">Jer 17:8</reference>). By the many waters which made the cedar great, we must not understand, either solely or especially, the numerous peoples which rendered Assyria great and mighty, as the Chaldee and many of the older commentators have done. It must rather be taken as embracing everything which contributed to the growth and greatness of Assyria. It is questionable whether the prophet, when describing the flood which watered the cedar plantation, had the description of the rivers of Paradise in Gen 2:10. floating before his mind. Ewald and Hävernick think that he had; but Hitzig and Kliefoth take a decidedly opposite view. There is certainly no distinct indication of any such allusion. We meet with this for the first time from <reference osisRef="Ezek.31.8">Eze 31:8</reference> onwards. <div eID="gen15101" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15102" type="x-p"/> In <reference osisRef="Ezek.31.6-Ezek.31.9">Eze 31:6-9</reference> the greatness and glory of Asshur are still further depicted. Upon and under the branches of the stately tree, all creatures, birds, beasts, and men, found shelter and protection for life and increase (<reference osisRef="Ezek.31.6">Eze 31:6</reference>; cf. <reference osisRef="Ezek.17.23">Eze 17:23</reference> and <reference osisRef="Dan.4.9">Dan 4:9</reference>). In כּּל־גּוים רבּים, all kinds of great nations, the fact glimmers through the figure. The tree was so beautiful (ויּיף from יפה) in its greatness, that of all the trees in the garden of God not one was to be compared with it, and all envied it on that account; that is to say, all the other nations and kingdoms in God’s creation were far inferior to Asshur in greatness and glory. גּן אלהים is the garden of Paradise; and consequently עדן in <reference osisRef="Ezek.31.9">Eze 31:9</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ezek.31.16">Eze 31:16</reference>, and <reference osisRef="Ezek.31.18">Eze 31:18</reference> is also Paradise, as in Eze 28:13. There is no ground for Kliefoth’s objection, that if עדן be taken in this sense, the words “which are in the garden of God” will contain a superfluous pleonasm, a mere tautology. In <reference osisRef="Gen.2.8">Gen 2:8</reference> a distinction is also made between עדן and the garden in <hi type="italic">Eden</hi>. It was not all Eden, but the garden planted by Jehovah in Eden, which formed the real paradisaical creation; so that the words “which are in the garden of God” give intensity to the idea of the “trees of Eden.” Moreover, as Hävernick has correctly pointed out, there is a peculiar emphasis in the separation of בּגן אלהים from ארזים in <reference osisRef="Ezek.31.8">Eze 31:8</reference> : “cedars...even such as were found in the garden of God.” Not one even of the other and most glorious trees, viz., cypresses and planes, resembled the cedar Asshur, planted by God by many waters, in its boughs and branches. It is not stated in so many words in <reference osisRef="Ezek.31.8">Eze 31:8</reference> and <reference osisRef="Ezek.31.9">Eze 31:9</reference> that the cedar Asshur stood in the garden of God; but it by no means follows from this, that by the garden of God we are to understand simply the world and the earth as the creation of God, as Kliefoth imagines, and in support of which he argues that “as all the nations and kingdoms of the world are regarded as trees planted by God, the world itself is quite consistently called a garden or plantation of God.” The very fact that a distinction is made between trees of the field (<reference osisRef="Ezek.31.4">Eze 31:4</reference> and <reference osisRef="Ezek.31.5">Eze 31:5</reference>) and trees of Eden in the garden of God (<reference osisRef="Ezek.31.8">Eze 31:8</reference> and <reference osisRef="Ezek.31.9">Eze 31:9</reference>), shows that the trees are not all regarded here as being in the same sense planted by God. If the garden of God stood for the world, where should we then have to look for the field (השּׂדה)? The thought of <reference osisRef="Ezek.31.8">Eze 31:8</reference> and <reference osisRef="Ezek.31.9">Eze 31:9</reference> is not that “not a single tree in all God’s broad earth was to be compared to the cedar Asshur,” but that even of the trees of Paradise, the garden in Eden, there was not one so beautiful and glorious as the cedar Asshur, planted by God by many waters.
entries.6ccb16b4138c19f30ea6fdbb359635d566cfe7c6: <reference osisRef="Ezek.31.10-Ezek.31.14">Eze 31:10-14</reference> <div eID="gen15102" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s2">The Felling of this Cedar, or the Overthrow of Asshur on Account of Its Pride</title> <div sID="gen15103" type="x-p"/> Eze 31:10. <hi type="italic">Therefore thus said the Lord Jehovah, Because thou didst exalt thyself in height, and he stretched his top to the midst of the clouds, and his heart exalted itself in its height,</hi> Eze 31:11. <hi type="italic">I will give him into the hand of the prince of the nations; he shall deal with him: for his wickedness I rejected him.</hi> Eze 31:12. <hi type="italic">And strangers cut him down, violent ones of the nations, and cast him away: upon the mountains and in all the valleys his shoots fell, and his boughs were broken in pieces into all the deep places of the earth; and all the nations of the earth withdrew from his shadow, and let him lie.</hi> Eze 31:13. <hi type="italic">Upon his fallen trunk all the birds of the heaven settle, and all the beasts of the field are over his branches:</hi> Eze 31:14. <hi type="italic">That no trees by the water may exalt themselves on account of their height, or stretch their top to the midst of the clouds, and no water-drinkers stand upon themselves in their exaltation: for they are all given up to death into hell, in the midst of the children of men, to those that go into the grave.</hi> - In the description of the cause of the overthrow of Asshur which commences with יען אשׁר, the figurative language changes in the third clause into the literal fact, the towering of the cedar being interpreted as signifying the lifting up of the heart in his height, - that is to say, in his pride. In the first clause the tree itself is addressed; but in the clauses which follow, it is spoken of in the third person. The direct address in the first clause is to be explained from the vivid manner in which the fact presented itself. The divine sentence in <reference osisRef="Ezek.31.10">Eze 31:10</reference> and <reference osisRef="Ezek.31.11">Eze 31:11</reference> is not directed against Pharaoh, but against the Assyrian, who is depicted as a stately cedar; whilst the address in <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Ezek.31.10">Eze 31:10</reference></hi>, and the imperfect (future) in <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Ezek.31.11">Eze 31:11</reference></hi>, are both to be accounted for from the fact that the fall of Asshur is related in the form in which it was denounced on the part of Jehovah upon that imperial kingdom. The perfect אמר is therefore a preterite here: the Lord said...for His part: because Asshur has exalted itself in the pride of its greatness, I give it up. The form ואתנהוּ is not to be changed into ואתנהוּ, but is defended against critical caprice by the imperfect יעשׂה which follows. That the penal sentence of God is not to be regarded as being first uttered in the time then present, but belongs to the past, - and therefore the words merely communicate what God had already spoken, - is clearly shown by the preterites commencing with גּרשׁתּיהוּ, the historical tenses ויּכרתהוּ and ויּטּשׁהוּ, and the preterite נפלוּ, which must not be turned into futures in violation of grammar. גּבהּ בּקומה does not mean, to be high in its height, which would be a tautology; but to exalt itself (be proud) in, or on account of, its height. And in the same way is רוּם also affirmed of the heart, in the sense of exultation from pride. For the fact itself, compare Isa 10:5. אל גּוים does not mean God, but a powerful one of the nations, i.e., Nebuchadnezzar. אל is a simple appellative from אוּל, the strong one; and is neither a name of God nor a defective form for איל, the construct state of איל, a ram. For this defective form is only met with once in the case of איל, a ram, namely, in <reference osisRef="Job.42.8">Job 42:8</reference>, where we have the plural  אלים, and nowhere else; whereas, in the case of אל, אלים, in the sense of a strong one, the <hi type="italic">scriptio plena</hi> very frequently alternates with the <hi type="italic">defectiva</hi>. Compare, for example, <reference osisRef="Job.42.8">Job 42:8</reference>, where both readings occur just as in this instance, where many MSS have איל (vid., de Rossi, <hi type="italic">variae lectt. ad h. l.</hi>); also <reference osisRef="Exod.15.15">Exo 15:15</reference> and <reference osisRef="Ezek.17.13">Eze 17:13</reference>, אילי, compared with אלי in <reference osisRef="Ezek.32.21">Eze 32:21</reference>, after the analogy of נירי, <reference osisRef="2Sam.22.29">2Sa 22:29</reference>, and גּירים, 2Ch 2:16. עשׂו is not a relative clause, “who should treat him ill,” nor is the w <hi type="italic">relat</hi>. omitted on account of the preceding עשׂו, as Hitzig imagines; but it is an independent sentence, and יעשׂה is a forcible expression for the imperative: he will deal with him, equivalent to, “let him deal with him.” עשׂה ל, to do anything to a person, used here as it frequently is in an evil sense; compare Psa 56:5. בּרשׁעו-or כּרשׁעו, which Norzi and Abarbanel (in de Rossi, <hi type="italic">variae lectt. ad. h. l.</hi>) uphold as the reading of many of the more exact manuscripts and editions - belongs to גּרשׁתּיהוּ: for, or according to, his wickedness, I rejected him. <div eID="gen15103" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15104" type="x-p"/> In <reference osisRef="Ezek.31.12">Eze 31:12</reference> the figure of the tree is resumed; and the extinction of the Assyrian empire is described as the cutting down of the proud cedar. זרים עריצי גּוים as in <reference osisRef="Ezek.28.7">Eze 28:7</reference> and <reference osisRef="Ezek.30.11">Eze 30:11</reference>-12. ויּטּשׁהוּ: they cast him away and let him lie, as in <reference osisRef="Ezek.29.5">Eze 29:5</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ezek.32.4">Eze 32:4</reference>; so that in the first sentence the idea of casting away predominates, and in the second that of letting lie. By the casting away, the tree became so shattered to atoms that its boughs and branches fell upon the mountains and on the low ground and valleys of the earth, and the nations which had sat under its shadow withdrew. ויּרדוּ (they descended) is to be explained from the idea that the three had grown upon a high mountain (namely Lebanon); and Hitzig is mistaken in his conjecture that ויּרדוּ was the original reading, as נדד, to fly, is not an appropriate expression for עמּים. On the falling of the tree, the birds which had made their nests in its branches naturally flew away. If, then, in <reference osisRef="Ezek.31.13">Eze 31:13</reference>, birds and beasts are said to settle upon the fallen trunk, as several of the commentators have correctly observed, the description is based upon the idea of a corpse, a מפּלת (Jdg 14:8), around which both birds and beasts of prey gather together to tear it in pieces (cf. <reference osisRef="Ezek.32.4">Eze 32:4</reference> and <reference osisRef="Isa.18.6">Isa 18:6</reference>). היה אל, to come towards or over any one, to be above it. The thought expressed is, that many nations took advantage of the fall of Asshur and rose into new life upon its ruins. - Eze 31:14. This fate was prepared for Asshur in order that henceforth no tree should grow up to the sky any more, i.e., that no powerful one of this earth (no king or prince) should strive after superhuman greatness and might. למען אשׁר is dependent upon גּרשׁתּיהוּ in <reference osisRef="Ezek.31.11">Eze 31:11</reference>; for <reference osisRef="Ezek.31.12">Eze 31:12</reference> and <reference osisRef="Ezek.31.13">Eze 31:13</reference> are simply a further expansion of the thought expressed in that word. עצי מים are trees growing near the water, and therefore nourished by water. For 'לא , see Eze 31:10. The words 'ולא יעמדוּ are difficult. As אליהם, with <hi type="italic">Tzere</hi> under א, to which the <hi type="italic">Masora</hi> calls attention, cannot be the preposition אל with the suffix, many have taken אליהם to be a noun, in the sense of <hi type="italic">fortes, principes</hi>, or <hi type="italic">terebinthi</hi> (vid., <reference osisRef="Isa.61.3">Isa 61:3</reference>), and have rendered the clause either <hi type="italic">ut non perstent terebinthi eorum in altitudine sua, </hi>o<hi type="italic">mnes (ceterae arbores) bibentes aquam</hi> (Vatabl., Starck, Maurer, and Kliefoth), or, that their princes may not lift themselves up in their pride, all the drinkers of water (Hävernick). But both renderings founder on the simple fact that they leave the suffix הם in אליהם either unnoticed or unexplained. As only the trees of the water have been spoken of previously, the suffix must be taken as referring to them. But the water-trees have neither terebinths nor princes; on the contrary, these are what they must either be, or signify. Terebinths, or princes of the water-trees, would be senseless ideas. Ewald has therefore taken אליהם as the object, and rendered it thus: “and (that) no water-drinkers may contend with their gods in their pride.” He has not proved, however, but has simply asserted, that עמד is to endure = to contend (!). The only remaining course is to follow the lxx, Targum, and many commentators, and to take אליהם as a pronoun, and point it אליהם. עמד אל: to station oneself against, or upon = עמד על (<reference osisRef="Ezek.33.26">Eze 33:26</reference>), in the sense of resting, or relying upon anything. The suffix is to be taken in a reflective sense, as in <reference osisRef="Ezek.34.2">Eze 34:2</reference>, etc. (vid., Ewald, §314 <hi type="italic">c</hi>), and precedes the noun to which it refers, as in <reference osisRef="Prov.14.20">Pro 14:20</reference> for example. בּגבהם, as in <reference osisRef="Ezek.31.10">Eze 31:10</reference>, referring to pride. כּל־שׁתי מים, the subject of the sentence, is really synonymous with כּל־עצי מים, except that the figure of the tree falls into the background behind the fact portrayed. The rendering of the Berleburg Bible is very good: “and no trees abounding in water stand upon themselves (rely upon themselves) on account of their height.” The water-drinkers are princes of this earth who have attained to great power through rich resources. “As a tree grows through the moisture of water, so men are accustomed to become proud through their abundance, not reflecting that these waters have been supplied to them by God” (Starck). The reason for this warning against proud self-exaltation is given in <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Ezek.31.14">Eze 31:14</reference></hi> in the general statement, that all the proud great ones of this earth are delivered up to death. כּלּם, all of them, the water-drinkers or water-trees already named, by whom kings, earthly potentates, are intended. ארץ תּחתּית = ארץ תּח (<reference osisRef="Ezek.26.20">Eze 26:20</reference>). בּתוך בּני אדם: in the midst of the children of men, i.e., like all other men. “Thus the prophet teaches that princes must die as well as the people, that death and decomposition are common to both. Hence he takes all ground of proud boasting away” (Starck).
entries.9e0c51d38c3630f0fc55ed74d5fc25378e72d104: <reference osisRef="Ezek.31.15-Ezek.31.18">Eze 31:15-18</reference> <div eID="gen15104" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s2">Impression Made upon the Nations by the Fall of Asshur; and Its Application to Pharaoh</title> <div sID="gen15105" type="x-p"/> Eze 31:15. <hi type="italic">Thus saith the Lord Jehovah, In the day that he went down to hell I caused a mourning: covered the flood for his sake, and stopped its streams, and the great waters were held back: I caused Lebanon to blacken itself for him, and all the trees of the field pined for him.</hi> Eze 31:16. <hi type="italic">I made the nations tremble at the noise of his fall, when I cast him down to hell to those who go into the grave: and they comforted themselves in the nether world, even all the trees of Eden, the choice and most beautiful of Lebanon, all the water-drinkers.</hi> Eze 31:17. <hi type="italic">They also went with him into hell, to those pierced with the sword, who sat as his helpers in his shade among the nations.</hi> Eze 31:18. <hi type="italic">Whom dost thou thus resemble in glory and greatness among the trees of Eden? So shalt thou be thrust down to the trees of Eden into the nether world, and lie among uncircumcised ones with those pierced with the sword. This is Pharaoh and all his tumult, is the saying of the Lord Jehovah.</hi> - In order that the overthrow of the Assyrian, i.e., the destruction of the Assyrian empire, may be placed in the clearest light, a picture is drawn of the impression which it made upon the whole creation. There is no necessity to understand כּה אמר in a past sense, as in Eze 31:10. What God did on the overthrow of Asshur He may even now, for the first time, make known through the prophet, for a warning to Pharaoh and the people of Israel. That this is the way in which the words are to be interpreted, is evident from the use of the perfect האבלתּי, followed by the historical imperfects, which cannot be taken in a prophetical sense, as Kliefoth supposes, or turned into futures. It is contrary to Hebrew usage to connect האבלתּי and כּסּתי together as <hi type="italic">asyndeton</hi>, so as to form one idea, viz., “to veil in mourning” as Ewald and Hävernick propose. The circumstances under which two verbs are joined together to form one idea are of a totally different kind. In this instance האבלתּי is placed first as an absolute; and in the sentences which follow, it is more specifically defined by a detail of the objects which were turned into mourning. כּסּה עליו את־תּהום cannot mean her, “to cover the flood upon (over) him” (after <reference osisRef="Ezek.24.7">Eze 24:7</reference> and <reference osisRef="Ezek.26.19">Eze 26:19</reference>); for this is altogether unsuitable to either the more remote or the more immediate context. The tree Asshur was not destroyed by a flood, but cut down by strangers. The following clauses, “I stopped its streams,” etc., show very plainly that the connection between the flood (תּהום) and the tree which had been felled is to be understood in accordance with Eze 31:4. A flood, which poured its נהרות round about its plantation, made the cedar-tree great; and now that the tree has been felled, God covers the flood on its account. כּסּה  is to be explained from כּסּה שׂק, to veil or wrap in mourning, as Raschi, Kimchi, Vatablus, and many others have shown. The word שׂק is omitted, because it appeared inappropriate to תּהום. The mourning of the flood is to be taken as equivalent to drying up, so that the streams which issued from it were deprived of their water. Lebanon, i.e., the cedar-forest (<reference osisRef="Isa.10.34">Isa 10:34</reference>), and all the other trees, mourned over the fall of the cedar Asshur. הקדּיר, to clothe in black, i.e., to turn into mourning. עלפּה is regarded by Ewald as a <hi type="italic">Pual</hi> formed after the Aramean mode, that is to say, by attaching the syllable <hi type="italic">ae</hi> instead of doubling the middle radical; whilst Hitzig proposes to change the form into עלּפּה. In any case the word must be a perfect <hi type="italic">Pual</hi>, as a <hi type="italic">nomen</hi> <hi type="italic">verbale</hi> appears unsuitable; and it must also be a third person feminine, the termination ־ה being softened into ־ה, as in זוּרה (<reference osisRef="Isa.59.5">Isa 59:5</reference>), and the doubling of the ל being dropped on account of the <hi type="italic">Sheva</hi>; so that the plural is construed with the singular feminine (Ewald, §317 <hi type="italic">a</hi>). עלּף, to faint with grief (cf. <reference osisRef="Isa.51.20">Isa 51:20</reference>). The thought is the following: all nature was so painfully affected by the fall of Asshur, that the whole of the resources from which its prosperity and might had been derived were dried up. To interpret the different figures as specially relating to princes and nations appears a doubtful procedure, for the simple reason that in <reference osisRef="Ezek.31.16">Eze 31:16</reference> the trembling of the nations is expressly named. <div eID="gen15105" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15106" type="x-p"/> Whilst all the nations on the surface of the earth tremble at the fall of Assyria, because they are thereby warned of the perishable nature of all earthly greatness and of their own destruction, the inhabitants of the nether world console themselves with the thought that the Assyrian is now sharing their fate (for this thought, compare <reference osisRef="Ezek.32.31">Eze 32:31</reference> and <reference osisRef="Isa.14.9-Isa.14.10">Isa 14:9-10</reference>). “All the trees of Eden” are all the powerful and noble princes. The idea itself, “trees of Eden,” is explained by the apposition, “the choice and beautiful ones of Lebanon,” i.e., the picked and finest cedars, and still further strengthened by the expression כּל־שׁתי  (cf. <reference osisRef="Ezek.31.14">Eze 31:14</reference>). מבחר are connected, as in <reference osisRef="1Sam.9.2">1Sa 9:2</reference>; and both words are placed side by side in the construct state, as in <reference osisRef="Dan.1.4">Dan 1:4</reference> (cf. Ewald, §339 <hi type="italic">b</hi>). They comfort themselves because they have gone down with him into Sheol, so that he has no advantage over them. They come thither to those pierced with the sword, i.e., to the princes and peoples whom Asshur slew in wars to establish his imperial power. וּזרעו might also belong to ירדוּ as a second subject. In that case ישׁבוּ בצלּו should be taken in a relative sense: “and his arm,” i.e., his resources, “which sat in his shadow among the nations.” With this explanation זרעו would be different from הם, and could only denote the army of the Assyrian. But this does not harmonize with the sitting in his shadow among the nations, for these words obviously point back to <reference osisRef="Ezek.31.6">Eze 31:6</reference>; so that זרעו is evidently meant to correspond to כּּל־גוים רבּים (<reference osisRef="Ezek.31.6">Eze 31:6</reference>), and is actually identical with הם, i.e., with all the trees of Eden. We therefore agree with Osiander, Grotius, and others, in regarding the whole of the second hemistich as more precisely determining the subject, - in other words, as a declaration of the reason for their descending into hell along with the Assyrians, - and render the passage thus: “for as his arm (as his might) they sat in his shadow among the nations;” so that the cop. w is used in place of a causal particle. In any case, the conjecture which Ewald has adopted from the lxx and the Syriac, viz., וזרעו, and his seed, in support of which appeal might be made to <reference osisRef="Isa.14.21">Isa 14:21</reference>, is unsuitable, for the simple reason that the statement, that it sat in his shadow among the nations, does not apply. - After this description of the greatness and the destruction of the imperial power of Assyria, Ezekiel repeats in <reference osisRef="Ezek.31.18">Eze 31:18</reference> the question already asked in <reference osisRef="Ezek.31.3">Eze 31:3</reference> : to whom is Pharaoh like? כּכה, so, i.e., under such circumstances, when the glorious cedar Asshur has been smitten by such a fate (Hitzig). The reply to this question is really contained in the description given already; so that it is immediately followed by the announcement, “and thou wilt be thrust down,” etc. ערלים, uncircumcised, equivalent to ungodly heathen 'הוּא פ, not “he is,” as that would require פּרעה הוּא; but הוּא is the predicate: this is (i.e., so does it happen to) Pharaoh. המונו, as in Eze 31:2.  <chapter eID="Ezek.31"/>
